prompt: You're on-site at Mount Rushmore negotiating the exact placement of your new carved face with a skeptical granite contractor who thinks the mountain is full. Write the negotiation. Stay in the scene.
response:
“I’m telling you,” the contractor said, tapping the rolled-up survey map against his hard hat, “the mountain is full.”

Wind dragged dust off the granite ledges and sent it skittering around our boots. Four enormous faces looked out past us, indifferent and already seated at the table forever.

I squinted up at the slope. “Full is a strong word.”

“Granite is a strong material.”

“You’ve got a little space there.”

He didn’t turn. “That is Washington’s collar.”

“I wasn’t suggesting the collar.”

“You pointed at the collar.”

“I gestured broadly in a spirit of collaboration.”

The contractor unrolled the map against a waist-high block of stone and pinned one corner with a thermos. Red pencil lines covered the paper like a nervous system.

“Here,” he said, stabbing the page. “Existing heads. Sightlines. Fracture zones. Drainage. Tourist viewing angle. Historical balance.”

“Historical balance?”

He looked up at me. “You want your face next to Lincoln?”

“I’m open to tasteful adjacency.”

“Everybody’s open to tasteful adjacency until they’re a seventy-foot cheekbone shedding ice onto the visitors’ center.”

A harnessed worker above us called something down. The contractor lifted one hand without looking, waited for the echo to settle, then pointed at the mountain.

“See that seam?”

I followed his finger. “The vertical one?”

“The one that says no.”

“It says no?”

“In granite, yes.”

I took two steps left, trying a different angle. From here, the presidents seemed less like faces and more like terrain that had once been persuaded to resemble men.

“What about lower?” I said. “Under Jefferson?”

The contractor stared at me.

“Not under-under,” I said. “Offset. A respectful lower-third placement.”

“You want to be a subtitle?”

“I want to be included.”

“Mount Rushmore is not a group photo at a wedding.”

A bus hissed somewhere below. Tiny tourists moved along the railings, raising phones toward the cliff. None of them knew history was being renegotiated by two men in safety vests standing beside a compressor.

I unzipped the tube under my arm and slid out the artist’s rendering. The paper snapped in the wind. There I was: dignified brow, heroic gaze, hair rendered more generously than nature had managed lately.
